title: Ngare Ndare Forest: Canopy Walk, Blue Pools and the Elephant Corridor to Lewa
meta_title: Ngare Ndare Forest Day Trip: Canopy Walk and Blue Pools
meta_description: Ngare Ndare Forest guide: canopy walk, blue pools, fees, getting there from Nanyuki and how to add it to a Laikipia safari in Kenya. Plan your visit.
excerpt: Ngare Ndare Forest, on the northern slopes of Mount Kenya, offers a canopy walkway, waterfalls and turquoise pools. Here is how to get there, when to go and how to add it to a Laikipia safari.
content:
Ngare Ndare Forest is an indigenous forest on the northern slopes of Mount Kenya, between Timau and Lewa, best known for a canopy walkway, turquoise rock pools and waterfalls you can swim under. Most visitors give it a morning or a full day from Nanyuki, Ol Pejeta or Lewa, walking with a trust guide.

The trouble is that most of what you read about it is either a single-visit diary or a tour listing, and the practical answers are scattered: how rough the road is, what the walk to the pools involves, how fees work and how to fit it into a wider Kenya safari in Laikipia and the Mount Kenya region. This guide pulls those answers together, from the turn-off at Timau to the best hour for the pools, with an honest view of who will enjoy it and who should spend the time on another game drive.

Quick Facts

  • Where: Northern foothills of Mount Kenya, off the Nanyuki to Meru road just past Timau, bordering Lewa Wildlife Conservancy
  • Managed by: The Ngare Ndare Forest Trust, working with the Kenya Forest Service
  • Status: Part of the Mount Kenya World Heritage Site since the 2013 extension that added Lewa and Ngare Ndare
  • Highlights: Canopy walkway of about 450 m, blue pools and waterfalls, forest walks, birding, camping
  • Drive time: About 1 hour from Nanyuki; roughly 4 hours from Nairobi
  • Best hour: 8:00 to 10:00 in the morning, as the trust itself advises
  • Wet seasons: Long rains April to June, short rains November to December

What is Ngare Ndare Forest, and why does it matter?

Ngare Ndare Forest is a fenced indigenous forest reserve on the dry northern side of Mount Kenya, managed by a community trust. It matters because it is the link that lets elephants move between the mountain and the Laikipia and Samburu lowlands, and because it gives safari travellers a rare chance to explore on foot.

The name comes from Maa and is usually translated as "goat waters", a nod to the river that herders have used for generations. According to the Ngare Ndare Forest Trust, visitors come for forest walks and drives, bird watching, the canopy walkway, picnics, camping and even rock climbing. Reports from Kenyan media describe the trust taking over day-to-day management in 2009 under an arrangement with the Kenya Forest Service, with neighbouring communities sharing in the work and the income.

Ngare Ndare Forest looks nothing like the open plains around it. Old African olive, pencil cedar and podo trees, some reckoned to be around two centuries old, close over the tracks, and the Ngare Ndare river cuts through volcanic rock into a chain of falls and pools. Sharing the forest with you are elephants, buffaloes, bushbuck, olive baboons and black-and-white colobus monkeys, with leopard present but rarely seen.

Is Ngare Ndare part of the Mount Kenya World Heritage Site?

Yes. In 2013 the World Heritage Committee approved the extension of the Mount Kenya World Heritage Site to include Lewa Wildlife Conservancy and Ngare Ndare Forest Reserve. The decision singles out a 9.8 km elephant corridor that connects the mountain to the Lewa and Ngare Ndare section, and stresses that keeping it open is critical. UNESCO's announcement of the extension put the added area at a core of nearly 20,000 hectares with a buffer zone of almost 70,000 hectares.

How do you get to the forest from Nanyuki?

You reach Ngare Ndare Forest by road from Nanyuki in about an hour: follow the tarmac towards Meru as far as Timau, turn off just past the town onto a rough track, drive about 11 km to the gate and then about 4 km inside the forest to the canopy walkway and blue pools.

The trust's own directions to Ngare Ndare Forest are precise. You turn left immediately after Timau, roughly 400 m beyond the police roadblock, and follow the signpost onto the murram road. A saloon car can get you to the forest, but the trust recommends a 4x4 for the waterfall tracks, and in the April to June or November to December rains a 4x4 stops being optional. Inside the forest the speed limit is 40 km/h and you stay on the marked tracks.

From Nairobi the drive is roughly four hours each way, which is why we rarely suggest it as a stand-alone day trip. Travellers already based around Nanyuki, Timau, Ol Pejeta or Lewa are the ones who get the most out of it, because they can arrive at the gate early. If you are flying in, the scheduled flights to Nanyuki cut the journey north to well under an hour, and a vehicle can meet you at the airstrip.

Do you need to book ahead?

The trust asks visitors to book in advance, and its office takes bookings from 8:00 to 17:00 on weekdays and 8:00 to 13:00 at weekends. That matters if you are planning a Saturday or Sunday visit at short notice. Guides and rangers are allocated from the booking, so arriving unannounced with a large group can mean waiting at the gate.

What can you do at Ngare Ndare Forest?

The three things most people come for at Ngare Ndare Forest are the canopy walkway, the walk down to the waterfalls and the blue pools, and a swim. Birders, campers and climbers can easily fill a second day.

The Ngare Ndare canopy walkway

The Ngare Ndare Forest canopy walk is a suspended bridge of around 450 metres strung between platforms in the treetops near the main forest track. Published heights vary between sources, so think of it as high enough to look across the crowns of the olive and cedar trees and down onto the forest floor. It is a short, easy walk in terms of effort, but people with a real fear of heights sometimes turn back on the first section. Your guide will point out colobus monkeys and birds feeding at canopy level, which is the best reason to go slowly.

The waterfalls and blue pools

From the canopy area a guided trail follows the river down to the cascades and the famous turquoise pools. Accounts suggest around half an hour of walking from the canopy platform to the first falls, and a few kilometres in total if you start further back, with some steep, uneven sections on rock and roots. Good walking shoes make a bigger difference here than fitness. The colour of the water is at its best in sunshine, which is one more reason to arrive early before cloud builds over the mountain.

Can you swim at Ngare Ndare, and is it safe?

Swimming is allowed in the Ngare Ndare pools and is the highlight for many visitors. It is safe enough with sensible precautions: go with your guide, check the depth before jumping, and stay out after heavy rain, when the river rises and the water turns murky.

The water at Ngare Ndare Forest is cold, coming straight off a forested mountain at well over 1,500 m, and most people manage a few minutes before warming up on the sun-heated rock. Bring a towel and a dry layer in your day pack, and wear something on your feet if the rocks are slippery. Jumping from the higher ledges is something people do, but it is not a requirement of the day, and our advice for families is simply to swim from the shallow edges.

Walking in a forest with elephants and buffaloes is the other safety point. The animals are wild and the forest is their corridor, so walks go with a trust guide or armed ranger who knows where herds have been moving. Keep voices low, stay together, and do exactly what the guide says if you meet elephants on the trail.

When is the best time to visit Ngare Ndare Forest?

The best time to visit Ngare Ndare Forest is during the drier months, roughly January to March and July to October, and always early in the morning. The trust recommends arriving between 8:00 and 10:00, when the light is good, the air is cool for walking and wildlife is more active.

The trust describes two wet seasons at Ngare Ndare Forest: the long rains from April to June and the short rains in November and December. Rain does not close the forest, but it makes the murram road slippery, the trails to the falls muddy and the pools cloudy, and you may not get the turquoise colour that draws people in the first place. In the dry months the forest stays green while the plains below turn gold, which is a big part of its appeal. How do you fit Ngare Ndare into a Laikipia safari?

Ngare Ndare Forest works best as a half or full day inside a two to four night stay in Laikipia, with game drives at Ol Pejeta or Lewa on either side. It gives you a morning on foot between drives and costs very little extra driving time if you are already north of Nanyuki.

A pattern that works well is a morning game drive at Ol Pejeta on day one, the forest on day two with a picnic by the pools, and a final morning drive before heading north to Samburu or back to Nairobi. Our Ol Pejeta Conservancy guide explains what to expect there, from the rhino sanctuary to the chimpanzee sanctuary, and the Laikipia wilderness guide covers the wider plateau, including wild dogs and the conservancies further west.

Two of our trips fit the forest naturally. The 7 day Ol Pejeta, Meru and Samburu safari passes along the same Nanyuki to Meru road, so we can add a forest morning between Ol Pejeta and Meru. Travellers who want more time on foot can pair the forest with the 4 day Laikipia walking safari with Samburu guides, where camels carry the camp between sites. Climbers heading up Mount Kenya often use the forest as an easy acclimatisation day before or after the 8 day Mount Kenya climb and safari.

How much does a visit to Ngare Ndare cost?

A visit to Ngare Ndare costs the trust's entry fee, plus a guide or ranger charge for walks and a camping fee if you stay overnight. The trust sets different rates for Kenyan citizens, residents and non-residents, with reductions for children, students and larger groups.

The trust's website does not publish a current price list (checked November 2026), and the figures quoted in older articles and tour listings disagree with each other, so we do not repeat them here. Ask for the current rates when you book, or let us confirm them for your dates. On a Divulge itinerary the forest fees, guide and ranger are included in the quote, so there is nothing to pay at the gate. The forest is not a Kenya Wildlife Service park, so it is not covered by KWS tickets; our Kenya park fees guide explains how the national park and conservancy fees around it work.

Your other costs are transport and lunch. If you are staying on a conservancy, the forest usually replaces a game drive rather than adding to the bill, and many lodges will pack a picnic. Travellers from overseas should also remember that most nationalities need an electronic travel authorisation (eTA) for Kenya before they fly, so apply well before you travel.

Insider Tips

  • Arrive early: Be at the gate by 8:00 for the best light on the pools and cooler walking
  • Wear proper shoes: The trail to the falls is rocky and steep in places; trainers with grip are fine, sandals are not
  • Pack for a swim: Swimwear under your clothes, a quick-dry towel and a warm layer for afterwards
  • Leave plastic behind: Single-use plastic bottles are not allowed; bring a refillable bottle
  • Bring binoculars: Turacos and other forest birds feed at canopy height, close to the walkway
  • Travel with a 4x4: Saloon cars reach the forest, but the waterfall tracks need ground clearance

Who will enjoy Ngare Ndare most?

Ngare Ndare suits travellers who like to walk, swim and slow down: families with active children, couples on a longer Kenya trip, birders and anyone who has done a few days of game drives and wants to stretch their legs. It suits travellers with limited mobility, or anyone on a very short safari, far less well.

If you only have three days in Kenya, spend them in the Masai Mara or Amboseli and leave the forest for next time. If you have a week or more, Ngare Ndare Forest earns its place, especially if you are already heading to Ol Pejeta, Lewa, Samburu or Mount Kenya: a morning there adds variety that the plains cannot. It also sits comfortably alongside the outings in our guide to day trips from Nairobi for anyone who prefers walking to sitting in a vehicle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Ngare Ndare Forest worth visiting?

Ngare Ndare Forest is worth a visit if you want a break from game drives: a canopy walkway, turquoise rock pools you can swim in and a guided walk among old olive and cedar trees. It suits active travellers staying around Nanyuki, Ol Pejeta or Lewa, and it fills a morning or a full day without a long transfer.

How much does it cost to visit Ngare Ndare Forest?

Ngare Ndare Forest is run by the Ngare Ndare Forest Trust, which sets separate entry, camping and ranger charges for Kenyan citizens, residents and non-residents. The trust's website does not publish a current price list, so confirm the rates when you book. When Divulge Adventures plans the day, the forest fees are built into your quote.

Can you swim in the Ngare Ndare blue pools?

Swimming in the Ngare Ndare blue pools is allowed and is one of the main reasons people go. The water comes off the forested slopes and is cold even at midday, so most people swim for a few minutes and warm up on the rocks. Go with your guide, check the depth before jumping and skip it after heavy rain.

How do you get to Ngare Ndare Forest from Nanyuki?

Ngare Ndare Forest is about an hour's drive from Nanyuki. You follow the Nanyuki to Meru road to Timau, turn off just after the town onto a rough road marked by the trust's signpost, drive about 11 km to the gate and then roughly 4 km inside the forest to the canopy walkway and pools. A 4x4 is best for the waterfall tracks.

Can I do Ngare Ndare Forest as a day trip from Nairobi?

A day trip to Ngare Ndare Forest from Nairobi is possible but long, with roughly four hours on the road each way. It works far better as part of a Laikipia safari: spend two or three nights at Ol Pejeta, Lewa or near Nanyuki and give the forest a relaxed morning, which is also when the trust says light and wildlife are best.

Final Thoughts

Ngare Ndare Forest is the easiest way to add a morning on foot to a Laikipia safari: a canopy walk, old trees and a cold swim in turquoise pools inside a World Heritage Site. Get there early, ideally from a base somewhere in the north.

A long day out from Nairobi rarely does the forest justice.
